newsitem.title: TAIWAN: U.S. firm turns up heat in Taiwan nuclear showdown.
newsitem.headline: U.S. firm turns up heat in Taiwan nuclear showdown.

text.p: U.S. contractor General Electric turned up the heat in a political showdown over Taiwan's fourth nuclear power station, indicating it would seek compensation if construction were delayed beyond Wednesday.
GE served notice on state utility Taiwan Power Co (Taipower) that it would not extend a midnight (1600 GMT) deadline for starting work on the project, Taipower officials said.
"General Electric has given Taiwan Power a written notice stating its decision not to extend the deadline," utility vice president Lin Chin-chi told Reuters.
"This means GE would be able to seek compensation if parliament does not agree to support the project by midnight tonight," Lin said.

Despite GE's deadline, the fate of the US$4.1 billion power plant -- and GE's US$1.8 billion contract to supply its twin reactors and generators -- was not scheduled to be settled until a final parliamentary vote on Friday.
Parliament embarrassed Taipei in May by cancelling funds for the project but the state and Taipower have pushed ahead anyway, filing a formal appeal to parliament in June.
Parliament can make the cancellation stand only with a two-thirds vote of attending members on Friday.

Debate was to have begun on Tuesday but lawmakers from the opposition Democratic Progressive Party blocked any action by physically barring Premier Lien Chan from entering the building to explain the appeal and defend the project.
Taipower's Lin would not estimate how much GE might seek in compensation if the huge project is delayed beyond the contractual deadline, calling this a matter for the courts.
"The issue would become a legal problem for Taiwan Power, so we cannot estimate what a delay or cancel of the project would cost General Electric," Lin said.
GE officials declined to comment on the notice, standing by the strict "no comment" policy it has observed throughout the long showdown between Taiwan's parliament and the government.

Premier Lien, visibly angered by Tuesday's rebuff, said the move to bar him from parliament represented a "dark day" for Taiwan's fledgling democracy and denounced the use of force rather than reason.
Lien had planned to deliver a report explaining Taiwan's energy policy and the island's need for the 2,700-megawatt nuclear plant, its fourth nuclear station.
Analysts have been reluctant to say whether opponents could muster the votes necessary to make the cancellation stand.
Taipower, which has continued with work despite the deadlock and regards the nuclear project alive unless a final rejection is approved, asked GE in September to start work.
The utility, calling the plant necessary and safe, already has poured more than US$220 million into its construction.
Taiwan approved the plant in 1994 after years of delays and protests sparked by the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster in the Soviet Union.
A growing number of opponents in increasingly democratic Taiwan say nuclear power is dangerous and unnecessary if alternative energy sources are pursued.
